The account would be challenged by evidence that the sense of self and its continuity remain intact when independently identified mechanisms of predictive self-modeling are abolished. The account does make some contact with possible evidence—if present experience were shown to be wholly unconditioned by past impressions, or if a fixed, unchanging self-substrate were somehow observed, that would count against it. But its central mechanisms (the store-consciousness and manas's self-grasping) are defined as subliminal and unrecognized in ordinary experience, so almost any introspective or behavioral finding, including the felt absence of such processes, can be absorbed rather than counted as disconfirming.

The account makes several empirically testable commitments—that predictive priors shape perception below awareness, that a self-model integrates bodily and sensory signals, and that the sense of I depends on this ongoing modeling—which predict, for example, that disrupting bodily integration or prior expectations (via illusions, lesions, or pharmacology) should measurably alter self-experience, and failures of such manipulations would count against it. However, its central claims about the "sense of being an I" and the absence of a fixed self are partly phenomenological and interpretive, so some core elements could absorb conflicting findings without clear refutation.

The account does entail some checkable consequences—present experience should be shaped by past impressions, and the sense of I should waver or lapse when the moment-to-moment appropriation is disrupted (e.g., in certain meditative or dissociative states)—so observations bearing on these could in principle count against it. However, its central mechanisms (a subliminal store-consciousness and an unrecognized self-grasping function) are defined as operating below awareness, which makes any failure to observe them compatible with the theory and leaves its core posits largely insulated from disconfirmation.
